Chapter 1: Leaving Home and the Weight of Expectation
Leaving home isn’t just about stuffing clothes into a suitcase or booking a flight. For so many people heading from East to West, that journey truly starts long before the airport—even before the ticket is bought. It’s born in those quiet family talks, in the shared glances at the dinner table, and in the silent hopes that hover over every conversation.
You know, the idea of “going West” shines with this special kind of promise. Somewhere out there, beyond the horizon, there’s a place where life feels freer, where chances are everywhere, and where you might finally get to be yourself.
Picture this: a young woman, sitting at her kitchen table in a tiny apartment. All around her is the gentle hum of family life—her parents moving quietly through their evening routine. They’ve worked hard for years to give her a sense of stability. Now, as she fills out applications for universities in Europe and North America, her parents don’t say much. But their eyes linger on her papers, and the message is unmistakable—her journey isn’t just hers. It belongs to the whole family. Every sacrifice, every hour spent saving, every blend of pride and worry—it all comes together in her choice to leave.
For a lot of people, leaving home feels like both an escape and a burden. There’s excitement, sure, but also a kind of guilt that’s hard to shake. The ones who stay behind hold on to their own silent dreams, hoping the person who leaves will make it—and somehow prove that all those sacrifices were worth it. Meanwhile, the traveler finds themselves torn—grateful for the chance, but scared to let anyone down.
Stories like these are at the heart of this book. The first steps toward the West are never just about geography—they’re full of anticipation and responsibility. Imagine a father, quietly slipping his son a small envelope at the airport. Inside, there’s a note, written carefully: “Make us proud, but don’t lose yourself.” Those words? They’re comforting, but they’re heavy too.
If you think about it, migration is almost never a solo act. Even if you’re the only one on that plane, you’re carrying the hopes of your parents, your siblings, maybe even your whole community. The dream of the West isn’t just about what you want—it’s about honoring a collective hope, shaped by stories of others who’ve gone before you. Sometimes those stories are wildly optimistic. Other times, they’re heartbreakingly true. Either way, they paint the West as a place where hard work pays off and old limits fade away.
But here’s something to pay attention to: underneath all that hope, there’s a steady current of anxiety. What if the new world isn’t as welcoming as you imagined? What if the dream falls apart? These worries don’t usually come up in the last-minute rush to pack, but they’re always there, in the background, coloring every decision.
As the plane finally takes off, the traveler looks out the window, watching the world they’ve always known slowly disappear. There’s a pang of loss, but there’s also this spark of hope. Most people don’t realize just how much invisible baggage comes along on that journey—the weight of expectations, the fear of failing, and the wish to fit in somewhere new, without losing touch with where you started.
In the end, going West isn’t just about crossing borders. It’s a leap into the unknown, powered by dreams that belong to both the individual and everyone rooting for them back home. This first chapter is written in the language of hope, anxiety, and the quiet courage it takes to step into the unknown—and leave everything familiar behind.
